name: Bayesian Reasoning Basics
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Updating Your Mind on Purpose: The Bayesian Habit
lesson.summary: Bayesian reasoning is the intuitive habit of starting from what you already believed, then adjusting that belief by an amount proportional to how strong and how surprising new evidence really is, rather than either ignoring new evidence or overwriting your prior belief completely every time something new appears.
lesson.body:
The disease test calculation in the base rate reasoning chapter was not just an example of base rates, it was a complete Bayesian update: you started with a prior belief, 1 percent, and used a new piece of evidence, a positive test, to move that belief to a posterior of about 16.7 percent. This chapter generalizes that same move into a habit of mind you can use on any claim, including ones that never come packaged with clean statistics.

There are three ingredients. Your prior is what you believed about the probability of a claim being true before this new piece of evidence arrived, based on the base rate and everything else you already know, including the field's general probability of success within a similar window of time. The strength of the new evidence is how much more likely that evidence would be to appear if the claim were true, compared to how likely it would be to appear if the claim were false. Your posterior is your updated belief, the honest combination of the two. The intuitive rule that falls out of this: strong evidence, meaning evidence that would be genuinely unlikely to occur if the claim were false, should shift your belief a lot. Weak evidence, meaning evidence that could easily show up either way, should shift your belief only a little, no matter how confidently it is presented.

Consider a quantum computing startup that announces it has achieved fault tolerant, error corrected qubits at scale, years ahead of every public roadmap. Your prior should start low, given the field's known base rate of similarly dramatic claims panning out on schedule and the field's general probability of success within any multi year window, not disbelief, but genuine, well founded skepticism, something like a small single digit percent. Now weigh the evidence. Is it a peer reviewed paper with data other researchers can independently check, or a company blog post timed conveniently around a funding round? A peer reviewed, independently reproduced result is evidence that would be unlikely to exist unless the claim were actually true, so it should move your belief substantially. A blog post from a company that stands to gain financially from the claim being believed is evidence that could easily appear whether or not the underlying claim is true, since companies make ambitious claims with some regularity regardless of the underlying reality, so it should move your belief only slightly. The exact same headline can and should produce very different posteriors depending on which kind of evidence is actually behind it.

A simple two question habit captures all of this without requiring heavy math in the moment: what did I believe before this specific piece of evidence, and how surprising would this evidence be if the claim were actually false? If the honest answer to the second question is not very surprising, this kind of claim gets made all the time and rarely holds up, then do not let the vividness of the announcement override that math. This habit is what turns skepticism, the subject of the next chapter, from a vague attitude into an actual, repeatable procedure you can run on any claim you meet.
